title.narrative: Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association Core Support
Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association Core Support

description.narrative: The Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association (ZELA) has been implementing the strengthening community-level governance frameworks for improved food security, climate resilience and environmental sustainability in Binga, Gutu, and Gwanda districts in Zimbabwe intervention through a 26.5 million SEK core support from Sida, October 2021-December 2024. The intervention aims at Strengthening community level governance frameworks for improved food security, climate resilience and environmental sustainability in Zimbabwe by 1) Strengthening institutional capacity of ZELA to contribute to sustainable natural resource governance and climate change resilience. ; 2) To strengthen the governance capacity of local level actors to drive sustainability of food security systems, climate resilience and natural resources management and ; 3) To strengthen the capacity of communities especially women and young people to influence the design and implementation of climate change and natural resource management policies. Through an amendment agreement to the core support with additional activities and funding of 4.5 million SEK, ZELA will continue the work started in 2021 for six months, ending 30 June 2025. The amendment was necessitated by the need to enhance sustainability of the beneficiaries in a changing climatic context as well as incorporating emerging issues such as competing land uses from enhanced critical raw material mining in Zimbabwe. The intervention’s total budget including the 4.5 million SEK added to the agreement amendment is 31 million SEK.

Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association (ZELA) har genom kärnstöd arbetat med att stärka samhällsstyrningen på lokal nivå för ökad livsmedelssäkerhet, stärkt resiliens mot klimateffekter samt varaktigt stärka miljön i Binga, Gutu, Gwanda, and Mbire districts in Zimbabwe från oktober 2021 till december 2024. Projektet syftar till att stärka samhällsstyrningen på lokal nivå för ökad livsmedelssäkerhet, stärkt resiliens mot klimateffekter samt varaktigt stärka miljön i Binga, Gutu, Gwanda, and Mbire districts in Zimbabwe genom att 1) stärka den institutionella kapaciteten hos ZELA för att de skall kunna bidra till uthållig hantering av naturresurser och resiliens mot klimatpåverkan; 2) öka förvaltningskapaciteten hos lokala aktörer för att stärka system för ökad livsmedelsäkerhet, resiliens i klimatfrågor och hantering av naturresurser; 3) stärka lokala samhällens förmåga, särskilt bland kvinnor och ungdomar, att få inflytande över utformning och genomförande av policies för klimatfrågor och hantering av naturresurser. Genom en avtalsändring kommer ZELA att motta ytterligare 4.5 MSEK för att dels fortsätta deras arbete som startade 2021, dels för att lägga till en del aktiviteter med avslut 30 juni 2025. Avtalsändringen var nödvändig för att säkerställa hållbarheten i projektet samt förmågan hos stödmottagarna i en ändrad kontext drabbad av klimatförändringar men också växande problemet med konkurrande markanvändning från gruvsektorn. Insatsens totala budget inklusive avtalsändringen på 4.5 MSK är 31 MSEK.

There are three main objectives to this intervention: Objective 1: To strengthen the governance capacity of local level actors to drive sustainability of food security systems, climate resilience and natural resources management.
Objective 2: To strengthen the capacity of communities especially women and young people to influence the design and implementation of climate change and natural resource management policies.
Objective 3: Strengthened institutional capacity of ZELA to contribute to sustainable natural resource governance and climate change resilience.
The intervention should result in poor and marginalised communities in Binga, Gutu and Gwanda becoming more resilient to climate change, improving their sustainable management of natural resources which will enhance their food security and move them towards poverty alleviation. The intervention should also result in the strengthening of ZELA at a time when it is paramount that local CSOs are capacitated and enhanced and are sustainable to meaningfully contribute to the country's development from an environmental lens.

Outcome 1: Functional Local-Level Institutions Sustainably Managing Climate Resilience Infrastructure and Natural Resources for Improved Food Security?
Transforming Irrigation Governance into Sustainable Climate-Resilient Institutions The project transformed local-level institutions (mainly irrigation schemes) in Gutu district (Ruti irrigation scheme) and Gwanda district (Silikwe, Bhopoma and Sukwe irrigation scheme), from fragile and conflict-ridden entities into functional, transparent, and productive structures.?The sustainability of climate adaptation measures was reinforced through the significant involvement and guidance of local government officials, embedding project outcomes within institutional structures for long-term impact. The irrigation schemes are now anchored on government policy and the law, as it relates to Climate Resilience infrastructure, Food security and broadly environmental sustainability. This makes it easy for the schemes to be recognised as part of the countrys agricultural architecture, ensuring continuity beyond project cycles. Government structures involvement in capacity strengthening of the irrigation schemes, made them functional in a sustainable manner, providing legitimacy, and regulatory enforcement power, and sustainability, which is essential for advancing climate change legal reforms and advocacy with evidence informed voices of irrigation schemes.
Breaking the Cycle of Water Resource based Conflict: Establishing Governance and Productivity Foundations The project played a pivotal role in defending and securing water tenure rights, particularly for women and young people, who are often the most excluded from decision-making over critical water resources. By promoting and operationalising the principles of Integrated Water Resource Management (IWRM), the project ensured that water governance shifted toward transparency, equity, and sustainability. Women and youth were not only protected as rights-holders but empowered as active participants in planning, allocation, and oversight of water resources. This strengthened community capacity to manage competing water demands, reduced conflicts, and enhanced climate resilience across districts. The integration of IWRM principles into local water structures has laid a durable foundation for inclusive, accountable, and climate-responsive water governance that will continue to safeguard water access and livelihoods well beyond the projects lifespan.
When the project began in 2022, irrigation schemes were beset by conflicts: 59% of farmers in district and 74% in Gwanda district, reported disputes and conflicts with Irrigation Management Committees (IMCs). Challenges notes as per the 2022 baseline (prior to project commencement), water conflicts, inequitable water resource access and allocation, poor financial management, political interference, and non-adherence to cropping calendars. Productivity was low, with average yields of 2 bags of maize, 11 buckets of beans, and 4 buckets of wheat per farmer per season. Women and youth, though active farmers, had limited influence in governance processes of the irrigation schemes, with communities not aware of the link between governance and improved agricultural outcomes.However, the project caused significant improvements to the situation., through investing in several capacity strengthening initiatives that empowered the irrigation scheme and the year 2022 marked the foundation stage, for realization of significant impact. The constitutions for the irrigation schemes were revised, leadership structures were reviewed, and IMCs demonstrated capacity in governance, financial management, and conflict resolution. By June 2025, 92.5% of surveyed farmers reported improved conflict management knowledge, and conflicts dropped significantly to 17% in Gutu district and 55% in Gwanda district.
From Water Resource Conflict to Productivity: Governance Improvements towards food security Productivity improvements significantly strengthened food security and household resilience across the irrigation schemes. At Ruti, farmers recorded harvests of up to 600 kg of beans per farmer, equivalent to USD 540 in gross income, demonstrating how strengthened governance directly translated into increased yields and stable food supplies. These gains were not accidental; they were the outcome of clearer constitutions, equitable water distribution, and transparent leadership systems that eliminated long-standing disputes and improved coordination at plot level. "We used to quarrel over water schedules, but now with the new and revised constitution, everyone knows their role and water is shared fairly," said Tendai Mudzimu, farmer at Ruti Irrigation scheme, Gutu district.
Such improvements ensured not only higher and more reliable production but also enhanced household nutrition, reduced vulnerability to climate shocks, and strengthened intergenerational well-being. Without these governance reforms, these transformative food security outcomes, including increased surplus production, improved income stability, and greater community cohesion, would not have been possible. The project testimony captures how productivity gains directly improved household resilience, reduced poverty and enhanced intergenerational well-being outcomes that would have been out of reach without stronger governance and institutional support.?
Governance Gains Driving Food Security, Climate Resilience, and Institutional Accountability By 2023-2024, the impact had deepened, with improved governance came greater productivity. By the end of June 2025, farmers now harvested an average of 10 bags of 50kg maize, 30 buckets of beans, and 20 buckets of wheat per season per farmer. Before this project, I barely produced enough to feed my family. Now, with 5 bags of maize and 30 buckets of beans per season, I sell the surplus and pay school fees for my children, shared Sibongile Ndlovu, Sukwe Irrigation farmer, Gwanda district.?
Transparency in management of the irrigation schemes improved, with IMCs providing regular financial updates. . The IMC now provides regular financial updates, effectively resolving financial disputes. The training on climate change has further equipped farmers to adapt and thrive. Ipaishe adds, I feel privileged to be part of this project. Ive applied what I learned to become resilient against climate shocks, and I expect a better harvest this season.
Gutu RDC demonstrated leadership by passing an environmental by-law in December 2023, incorporating community recommendations such as stiffer penalties for unsustainable land practices. In Binga district, a communication platform with ZimParks was created, allowing communities to quickly report and address Human-Wildlife Conflicts (HWC), a platform that was absent prior to project commencement. "In the past, if elephants destroyed our fields, we suffered in silence. Now we call ZimParks, and they respond in no time," explained John Munsaka, farmer from Tinde ward, Binga district. The creation of such responsive systems highlights how the project shifted relationships between communities and duty-bearers from neglect to accountability in wildlife governance.??
Sustainably Managing Climate Resilience Infrastructure and Natural Resources for Improved Food Security? Sida-supported infrastructure upgrades at Ruti Irrigation, including pump house construction and electrification, transforming irrigation reliability for 247 farmers in Gutu district, and directly boosting productivity and food security capacity and possibilities for Gutu district farmers. Sida support for the major infrastructure upgrades, included guidance planning processes for the upgrade, supported by an onsite visit that was done by both Sida and ZELA officials. The upgrade, which included pump house construction and electrification at Ruti Irrigation, are envisaged to benefit the 247 farmers at Ruti Irrigation scheme. Sida support not only enhanced governance and infrastructure, but also reduced unsafe night-time irrigation, mitigating gender-based violence risks whilst at the same time increasing yields and empowering women and young farmers
Farmers under the project, institutionalized sustainability through Savings and Internal Lending Committees (SILCs), pooling resources in Gutu district and Gwanda district, to maintain infrastructure and strengthen financial resilience and governance. The schemes shifted from subsistence to business-oriented enterprises, with 80% of farmers earning an average seasonal income of USD 750 compared to baseline subsistence levels. Improved irrigation functionality attracted significant external investment. Food and Agriculture Organisations (FAO's) support to Silikwe IMC and Governments planned Phase 4 expansion for Ruti irrigation scheme, signal recognition of the schemes as reliable and sustainable institutions.
Over the project lifespan, irrigation schemes in Gwanda district and Gutu district, thus shifted from dysfunction to climate resilient structure. Conflicts plummeted, productivity more than doubled, women gained safer working conditions, and local authorities became more responsive. Critically, these results show a pattern of transformation that would not have occurred without the project; without Sida's support, the irrigation schemes would likely still be sites of conflict, mismanagement, and stagnation. Instead, they are now vibrant, community-led institutions driving food security, equity, and climate resilience in Zimbabwe's most vulnerable districts.?
Outcome 2: Empowered Communities, Especially Women and Youth, Advocate for Inclusive Climate Change and Natural Resource Management (NRM) Policies?
Gender responsive Climate Change and Natural Resource advocacy The project successed in promoting inclusive environmental and climate advocacy among target communities in Gutu district and Gwanda district, with regards to women and youth, transforming them from passive observers into active shapers of environmental governance , including climate policy and NRM policies. This shift is important because historically, rural communities have been sidelined in environmental decision-making, with their lived realities rarely informing national policies. By breaking this pattern, the project ensured that climate and natural resource governance in Zimbabwe became more inclusive and responsive, with community voices especially of poor/marginalized women and youth.
Empowerment of women in IMCs became institutionalized through the project and beyond. Community monitors from Gutu district and Gwanda district reported 38 environmental cases to EMA and RDCs, who responded accordingly.? ZELA amplified womens voices nationally through the Women Ignite radio programme, positioning women as public advocates. Farmers and monitors engaged in Pre-COP 29 consultations, ensuring grassroots realities shaped national climate positions.?
From knowledge acquisition to active participation in decision making Communities in Binga district and Gwanda district, moved from acquiring knowledge to actively engaging in the policy and legal discourse, influencing both local and national decision-making. Women and youth emerged as leaders, environmental conflicts declined, and grassroots voices are now embedded in Zimbabwes natural resource governance frameworks. This is significant impact, since the project took out communities from a position of being marginalized as voiceless victims of climate change and environmental mismanagement and transformed them into agents of change, capable of shaping laws, influencing policies, and safeguarding their own futures.? One community member remarked: I now understand environmental law and climate change basics better than some people who went to university, even though I never had the opportunity to pursue higher education myself Chido (Pseudo name)
In 2022, capacity-building laid the foundation. ZELA empowered communities on Human and Wildlife Conflicts and Coexistence, sustainable wildlife management, environmental rights and broad Human Rights Based Approaches (HRBAs). Knowledge levels soared, with 99% retention on HWC, 88% on sustainable wildlife management, and 83% on climate change awareness, and there is evidence that the communities progressed to knowledge application in their farming conduct. These numbers matter because they demonstrate learning and readiness for communities to step into advocacy roles that were previously out of reach. Equipped with knowledge, communities began reporting offences: between JuneDecember 2022, 36 poaching cases, 68 HWC cases, and 8 problem animal incidents were reported to Binga RDC and ZimParks. At first, people laughed when I spoke about environmental laws because I am a woman. Now village heads call me to train others, and we have reduced tree cutting and veld fires, said Aganeta Maposa, Environmental Monitor, Ward 14, Gutu district, who reached 255 villagers through her own community meetings. Youths in Lubanda ward formed an Environmental Club led by young women, conducting clean-up campaigns and awareness drives targeting peers previously involved in poaching.?
Community voices into policy and legal processes By 20232024, empowerment translated into advocacy capacity and action. Communities directly influenced national policies, submitting inputs into the Parks and Wildlife Amendment Bill and the framework for community conservancies. They called for community ownership of conservancies, fair compensation for HWC losses, streamlined permits, and recognition of Indigenous Knowledge Systems. This was unprecedented: rural voices shaping national legal frameworks that directly affect their livelihoods.? Our voices are finally in Parliament. We asked for compensation when elephants destroy crops, because our survival depends on it, testified Memory Dube, from Binga district, after attending the public hearings. The project connected the local to the national and even global level, a link that would not exist without Sidas support. Farmers from Gutu district and Gwanda district participated in Pre-COP 27 consultations, influencing Zimbabwes position on Loss and Damage.?
Community-Led Conservation Gains: Reduced Wildlife Conflict and Rising Youth Environmental Stewardship At the community level, tangible changes emerged in poaching cases dropped from 36 in 2022 to 11 in 2023, while HWC incidents fell from 68 to 38, and problem animals from 8 to 2. Knowledge levels rose further; by December 2024, 91% of communities understood sustainable wildlife management, and 93% understood HWC. Youth-led E-Clubs expanded, leading clean-ups, tree planting, and environmental education campaigns. Through the establishment and support of 11 vibrant E-Clubs across Binga District, peer-to-peer learning and environmental stewardship were significantly advanced. These youth-driven platforms empowered learners to actively engage in environmental governance and climate justice, while spearheading clean-up campaigns, tree planting initiatives, and awareness activities on sustainable natural resource management.
By embedding environmental education into school culture at institutions including Tinde High, Saba Secondary, Mupambe Secondary, Siyanzundu High, Siachilaba Secondary, Simatelele High, Manjolo High, Binga High, Lubanda Secondary, Simbala Secondary, and Chasamba Secondary school, the project fostered a generation of environmentally conscious young leaders championing collective action for a sustainable future. The Ward Environmental Management Committee in Tinde petitioned for reclassification to a high-risk HWC zone, which has been under consideration for quite some time by the Binga Environmental Management Committee, demonstrating communities agency in pursuing tangible policy benefits. These voices would still be excluded, and conflicts with wildlife would continue to devastate livelihoods unchecked in the absence of this project.?
Building the Foundations for Just, Inclusive, and Climate-Smart Environmental Governance ZELA advanced environmental protection, climate resilience, and contributed to the pathway towards just energy governance by driving national and local action on water infrastructure improvements, as well as climate change mitigation and adaptation. The organisation played a pivotal role in shaping climate-responsive laws and policies, strengthening community capacity to adapt to climate shocks while influencing equitable energy transition frameworks aligned with Sida's sustainability objectives.
Outcome 3: Strengthened Institutional Capacity of ZELA to contribute to Sustainable Natural Resource Governance and Climate Change Resilience?
Human rights, democratic governance and accountability (including corruption reduction) Between 2021 and 2025, ZELA significantly advanced the human rights and democratic governance agenda within Zimbabwe and across the southern African region. Regionally, ZELA's leadership within SADC civil society platforms and participation in African Union policy dialogues elevated community and civil society perspectives on extractives, climate justice, and gender equality in natural resource governance ZELA played a key role in influencing SADC policy positions on critical minerals, corporate accountability, and rights-based ESG standards, aligning them with the African Mining Vision. Internationally, ZELA contributed to the Kimberley Process Civil Society Coalition (KP CSC), advocating for human rights-based diamond governance and fair benefit sharing in mineral value chains. Its active engagement with the OECD Responsible Business Conduct (RBC) platform positioned ZELA as a Southern voice advancing due diligence, labour rights, and environmental compliance in the mining sector.
Through Sida's core support, ZELA significantly elevated Zimbabwe's visibility and leadership on global environmental and governance platforms. The organisation presented at the OECD Responsible Mineral Supply Chain Forum (20232024), showcasing best practices in responsible lithium and gold governance, and co-authored civil society submissions on a just energy transition for UNFCCC COP27 and COP28. ZELA also made technical contributions to the United Nations Environment Assembly (UNEA), COP27, and COP28, where it amplified calls for equitable climate financing and the recognition of Environmental, Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights (EESCRs) as integral to climate justice. ZELA also contributed to the African Mining Vision (AMV) and SADC Green Growth dialogues, advancing gender-responsive, climate-aligned governance frameworks across the region.
Sida's support was instrumental in securing ZELA's recognition to participate in the UNFCCC Climate Change Negotiations in Bonn as part of the Government of Zimbabwe delegation, where it provided legal and policy advisory input. Furthermore, ZELA's appointment to the UNFCCC constituted bodies under Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement, which governs carbon credit mechanisms, firmly positioned the organisation as a trusted technical actor, aligning Sida-funded initiatives with Zimbabwe's obligations under international climate frameworks.
The organisations development of the National Gender, Climate, and Extractives Position Paper (2024) further strengthened women's policy representation in regional and international climate negotiations, including Zimbabwe's pre-COP29 submissions. Through these efforts, ZELA enhanced transparency, accountability, and gender equality in governance systems while influencing regional and global frameworks that uphold human rights, democracy, and the rule of law within extractives and climate governance spaces.
Strategic Partnerships and Resource Mobilisation The landmark donor conference that was convened in 2024 at Sida, and attracted over 40 strategic partners,including donors and CSOs, led to transformative partnerships with various funding partners. A typical example is the partnership with Hivos, which is envisaged to strengthen ZELO's urban environment programme. ZELA also co-hosted a Youth Climate Change Conference together with other Civil Society actors. Through sustained engagement with government agencies (Environmental Management Agency-EMA, Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Authority-ZIMPARKS, the National Prosecuting Authority-NPA, Rural District Councils-RDCs and AGRITEX) and civil society, ZELA expanded its institutional network, strengthened consortium building, which led to or unlocked new funding opportunities, positioning the organisation as a central driver, environmental steward and champion on natural resource governance.
Organisational Growth and Sustainability With Sida's strategic support, ZELA aligned its operations to the 20252029 Strategic Mandate, reinforcing accountability, impact orientation, and financial governance, building on the core support received from Sida during the 2020-2024 Strategic phase. Institutional reviews of MEAL and financial systems sharpened programmatic focus, enhanced media visibility, and improved resilience. Mid-term and annual review meetings strengthened responsiveness to emerging NRG challenges, while heightened visibility expanded opportunities for diversified funding streams, ensuring ZELAs long-term sustainability and leadership in the NRG space.
The systemic migration from Special Purpose Financial Reporting (SPFR) to a new accounting system, the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) reporting, is critical to ensuring that the organisations financial reporting is transparent, consistent, and aligned with globally and nationally recognised best practices. By adhering to IFRIS, ZELA can produce credible and comparable financial statements that build trust with donors, partners, regulators, and other stakeholders. Moreover, in an increasingly regulated environment, IFRIS compliance reduces the risk of legal or audit challenges, positioning ZELa as a responsible and trustworthy steward of resources, with a sound asset base that promotes it mobility and outreach to marginalised and vulnerable communities, dedicated to advancing its mission in localised NRG
The projects cornerstone lies in how it transformed ZELA into a solid, resilient, and credible institution capable of driving the natural resource governance and climate change discourse at local, national, regional, and global levels. Sida's investment in ZELA's systems, skills, and visibility ensured that the organisation could sustain impact, amplify grassroots voices, and shape policy far beyond the project sites. Without Sida's support, ZELA's work would likely have remained fragmented and under-resourced, but with Sida investment, the Organisation has become a recognised thought leader and partner of choice for both government and international actors.? In 2022, Sida investments laid the institutional foundation through comprehensive systems audits not only identified gaps, but also guided a comprehensive review of internal control systems, leading to stronger accountability and efficiency.
The systems strengthening and support was not limited to accounting systems, but it it extended to programming capacity strengthening. The core support grant financed two vehicles and modern office equipment, which expanded ZELA's ability to reach remote, resource-rich but marginalised communities in Binga district , Gutu district and Gwanda district. Importantly, Sida support funded the recruitment of specialised staffing positions that included a MEAL Officer, a Grants Compliance Officer, a Data Protection Officer, ESG Officer, and a Fundraising Officer, embedding critical expertise into ZELA's structure. Unlike short-term donor-funded posts, these roles are now entrenched in ZELA's organogram and fundraising strategy, a deliberate sustainability move.?
Participatory Evidence and Result-Oriented M&E of the environmental governance centred work of ZELA, facilitated for the development of sound M&E frameworks for policy and legal monitoring and review, that allow for real-time feedback and adaptation, accountability and learning, with community and multi-stakeholder. The impact assessments executed (internally and externally based), enabled timely adjustments to strategies and continuous improvement that ensured interventions were relevant and impactful.?
Sida support enabled ZELA to strengthen its Strategic programme areas, with special mention of two flagship portfolios, a solid Climate Change and Energy Governance Programme management unit, and a solid Land and Natural Resources Programme with a special thematic area on Wildlife programming. These thematic anchors have provided the organisation with a platform for long-term engagement and credibility in key policy spaces.? ZELA leveraged and continues to leverage on this stronger foundation to expand influence and recognition. With a staff complement of 25 in 2023 and 42 in 2024, ZELA now had the human capital to engage at scale. Increased media visibility attracted further donor funding in climate and wildlife programming.
The organisation managed to turn community-generated evidence into national advocacy products, amplifying grassroots experiences to influence reform of the Water Act and environmental policies.?ZELA's strengthened credibility led to unprecedented recognition by government institutions, for instance, the organisation was invited to contribute to the Harare City Council Climate Strategy, to lead a clause-by-clause review of Zimbabwe's Climate Change Bill, and to shape the Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill consultations. It represented Zimbabwean communities at the OECD Responsible Supply Chain Forum and the Alternative Mining Indaba. ZELA promoted responsible mining, environmental stewardship, and sustainable resource management, embedding transparency, social justice, and ecological integrity into extractives governance.
ZELA appointed the Legal Advisor for the Zimbabwean Elephant Management Committee by the Ministry of Environment and Parks and ZIMPARKS. The organisation was also appointed the legal technical member for the TFCAs fundraising committee for Zimbabwe and ZIMPARKS to spearhead the development of a legal and governance framework for community conservancies in Zimbabwe as well as spearhead the development of a HWC Conflict Relief Fund Policy.
Contribution to legal, policy and institutional reforms on NRG At the policy and institutional level, ZELA's research and advocacy have informed several key reforms, including the Climate Change Management Bill, the Water Act Review, and the development of local environmental by-laws that integrate climate adaptation, biodiversity conservation, and gender equality into governance frameworks, Legal and Technical Influence
ZELA's technical expertise shaped Harare's climate strategy and contribution to European Union (EU) wildlife projects, led to the organisation being recognised as a technical lead on climate and wildlife governance. High-level policy engagements with Harare Municipality and demand for consultancies from CSOs and development partners underscored ZELA's growing reputation as a trusted technical advisor and influential player in climate and natural resource programming nationally and regionally.
Below is a tabulatation of ZELA's influence on some of the legislative developments as elaborated below:
- Climate Change Management Bill? ZELA was tasked by the Ministry of Environment, Climate and Wildlife as the lead CSO expert to lead in the review of the draft Bill from the Attorney Generals office by identifying gaps, weaknesses, or provisions that may need to be revised, removed, or recast.? ZELA played a pivotal role in safeguarding environmental justice, strengthening climate governance, and ensuring that national law aligns with international best practices. This strategic engagement positioned ZELA at the centre of legislative reform, ensuring that community rights, climate resilience, and responsible natural-resource governance are embedded in Zimbabwe's emerging legal framework.
- Parks and Wildlife Management Bill? ZELA participated in the public consultations for the Bill and further supported the participation of environmental monitors from Binga, Hwange, Matopo, Gokwe, Tsholotsho for the Bill. This initiative assisted in addressing constraints, legal gaps, and opportunities for sustainable conservation practices.??
ZELA strengthened national wildlife governance by ensuring that communities most affected by conservation decisions, through environmental monitors from Binga, Hwange, Matopo, Gokwe, and Tsholotsho, actively shaped the Parks and Wildlife Management Bill, amplifying voices of the marginalized and helping address long-standing governance constraints, in the advancement of more inclusive, sustainable conservation frameworks that reflect real community needs and ecological priorities.
- Carbon Trading Regulations? ZELA produced an explainer of SI 48 of 2025 following its initial analysis of the repealed SI 158/2023.?ZELA significantly strengthened public understanding and transparency around Zimbabwe's emerging carbon market regulations. This intervention demystified complex legal provisions, empowered communities, civil society, and policymakers with accurate information, and contributed to more informed engagement on carbon governance. ZELA's work ensured that the transition from SI 158/2023 to SI 48/2025 did not deepen confusion, but instead enhanced accountability, clarity, and evidence-based dialogue on climate finance and carbon trading in Zimbabwe.
- Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill? Zimbabwe's ambitious USD 12 billion mining target positions the sector as a major economic driver. The current mining regime requires reform to facilitate mineral value without compromising environmental integrity. During the project period, a Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill was gazetted in 2023, but the Bill lapsed when Parliament dissolved for the 2023 general elections. A new Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill was gazetted on 25 June 2025 in the Government Gazette.?
ZELA played a critical role in shaping national mining governance at a pivotal moment, ensuring that ongoing reforms to the Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill aligned with principles of environmental protection, accountability, and community benefits, as Zimbabwe's mining sector grows, laying a sound foundation for continued advocacy for a more transparent, equitable, and environmentally responsible mining regime, that protects marginalised communities and ecosystems while supporting national economic ambitions.
- Accession to the 1992 Water Convention and the 1997 Watercourses Convention? Zimbabwe initiated accession to the 1992 Water Convention and the 1997 Watercourses Convention. ZELA participated in national workshop on the accession highlighting alignment of domestic laws with treaties, investment in groundwater, gender and social inclusion, and strengthened information management at transboundary levels, which were crucial to the project goal.? ZELA advanced critical issues of alignment of domestic water laws with international standards, investment in groundwater management, gender and social inclusion, and improved transboundary information system, thereby influencing a pathway to more equitable, sustainable, and climate-resilient water governance, directly advancing the projects goals.
- Evidence generation and Thought Leadership on Climate and Natural Resource Governance Through evidence-based advocacy and community-led interventions, ZELA strengthened the sustainable management of natural resources and biodiversity conservation. Its work enhanced accountability in land, water, and forestry governance, directly contributing to the Objective 2 under Sweden's bilateral strategy to Zimbabwe (2022-2026) on environmental sustainability and the responsible use of natural resources, ensuring that ecosystems are managed transparently and inclusively for long-term community benefit.
ZELA produced cutting-edge research on carbon credits and showcased its influence at platforms such as the Africa Voluntary Carbon Market Forum and SADC Industrialisation Week. ZELA led the clause-by-clause review of the Climate Change Bill on behalf of the Ministry of Environment and provided technical expertise to the Ministry of Mines on the Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill. These interventions cemented ZELA's role as a thought leader and legal reform champion, shaping policy and practice in Zimbabwe and beyond.
ZELA is recognised as an expert by organisations such as BIOHUB and CIRAD. Most notably, ZELA was appointed by ZIMPARKS and the Ministry of Environment as the Legal Advisor for the Zimbabwean Elephant Management Committee and as the legal technical member of the TFCA (Transfrontier Conservation Area) Fundraising Committee for Zimbabwe. These roles signalled that ZELA had become a trusted advisor on some of the countrys most sensitive and strategic governance issues and structures.?
In 2025, ZELA has been consolidating its role as a national and global thought leader. ZELA, at the request of ZIMPARKS, spearheaded the development of a governance framework for community conservancies, made input to the Human-Wildlife Conflict Relief Fund Policy, and contributed to the drafting of Zimbabwes Wildlife Policy.?
The achievements of ZELA were backed by formalised partnerships for the sustainability of partnerships beyond the project period. Remarkably, ZELA signed Memoranda of Understanding with ZIMPARKS, the National Prosecuting Authority, Zimbabwe Republic Police CID Minerals Flora and Fauna Unit, the International Foundation for Animal Welfare (IFAW), Zimbabwe Women in Conservation Association, International Animal Advocates, and the Wildlife Conservation Association. These MoUs institutionalised collaboration, ensuring that ZELA's influence was not ad hoc but part of formal governance frameworks.?
The Sida support enabled ZELA to operationalise policies that reinforced resilience internally, such as the Working from Home Policy introduced during COVID-19 disruptions. This flexible adaptation proved critical in maintaining productivity while positioning ZELA as a modern and resilient employer.?
The broader impact of the organisations institutional strengthening has been profound. Sida transformed ZELA from a strong implementer into a strategic convener, technical advisor, and empowered policy influencer. ZELA's ability to turn community-generated evidence into policy influence is now unmatched. Farmers and environmental monitors reports are feeding directly into legislative reforms such as the Climate Change Bill and Water Act. The organisations role in pushing for the establishment of Environmental Courts demonstrates how it is shaping long-term accountability structures in the country.?
ZELA has become an indispensable actor in Zimbabwe's governance architecture, trusted by communities, civic actors, the government and the donor world, respected by international organisations, with a deep grounding in global climate processes. Sida's deliberate investment in both systems and programmes ensured ZELA's sustainability. To date, specialised staff, thematic programmes, and partnerships are fully institutionalised, guaranteeing that the impact of this project will continue beyond Sidas direct support.? Through Sida's grant, ZELA was also able to extend institutional support to the?Africa Institute of Environmental Law (AIEL), a regional think tank established by ZELA that operates across Southern Africa. Sida's support strengthened AIEL's capacity to deliver high-quality research, policy analysis, and advocacy on critical issues such as climate governance, environmental justice, and natural resource management. With this backing, AIEL has grown in visibility and credibility, positioning itself as a?thought leader in the region?and a go-to think tank when it comes to environmental law and natural resources governance, leading to it being a trusted partner for governments, civil society, and international platforms.?
The project demonstrated a clear incremental impact trajectory from 2022 and 2025. Irrigation schemes evolved from conflict-ridden to productive, transparent institutions, and whilst they were getting transformed, ZELA was also learning, adapting and renewing its delivery approaches and strategies. Communities, women, and youth moved from knowledge acquisition to policy influence and measurable reductions in resource-based conflicts, whilst ZELA grew from an implementer to a nationally recognised, a regionally recognised policy and legal influencer. The evidence speaks volumes, and by coupling local institution-building with community empowerment and institutional strengthening, Sida enabled sustainable outcomes on security, climate resilience and environmental sustainability in Binga district, Gutu district, and Gwanda district, that will outlive the project phase. This integrated model strengthened governance, empowered communities, and capacitated institutions, offering a replicable blueprint for advancing climate resilience and natural resource governance in Zimbabwe and broadly the African region, in applicable contexts. Through Sida's support, "ZELA has become a voice not just for communities, but with communities, in shaping laws that affect their daily lives," remarked Mutuso Dhliwayo, Executive Director of ZELA.?
- Influence on responsible economic development through strengthened private sector engagement In relation to the mining sector, ZELA's advocacy for Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) compliance and its partnerships with mining stakeholders, including the Chamber of Mines, drove adoption of responsible business practices among at least 10 companies, aligning corporate behaviour with Economic, Environmental, Social and Cultural Rights (EESCRs).
ZELA also advanced responsible economic development by promoting inclusive governance and accountability within agricultural value chains. Through targeted training on grievance redress mechanisms, ZELA capacitated the Ruti Irrigation Management Committee (IMC) to expand its existing disciplinary committee into a fully functional Grievance Redress Committee, enabling it to address not only internal disputes but also grievances from external stakeholders and third parties. This transformation strengthened transparency, social accountability, and trust between farmers, local institutions, and private partners.
Building on this success, ZELA facilitated knowledge exchange between the Ruti Irrigation Scheme and Green Fuel, one of Zimbabwe's leading private sector actors in the bio-energy sector. Inspired by Ruti's inclusive governance model, Green Fuel expressed commitment to expand its operational scope beyond Manicaland, contingent on funding availability, to replicate sustainable agricultural practices in other regions. This engagement demonstrates how ZELA's facilitation of equitable partnerships can leverage private sector investment toward socially responsible, inclusive, and environmentally sustainable economic growth.
- Building Robust Institutions for Responsible and Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) -Aligned Mining
ZELA advanced ESG and environmental safeguards with a base of over 200 artisanal and small-scale miners empowered by ZELA on ESG standards, occupational safety, and responsible sourcing. The organisation commissioned an ESG Scoping Study under the project, focused on critical minerals, specifically lithium, gold, and granite, to strengthen corporate accountability and sustainable mining practices. The study provided a comprehensive analysis of the sectors challenges and opportunities, highlighting persistent issues such as environmental degradation, social inequities, and governance weaknesses, and underscored the urgent need for reform through ethical and sustainable procurement. Key findings emphasized the importance of integrating materiality into ESG frameworks to better address stakeholder needs and enhance transparency in reporting. The study recommended modernising and enforcing regulatory frameworks, building institutional capacity, and fostering multi-stakeholder collaboration among mining companies, government bodies (including the Zimbabwe Investment and Development Agency), civil society, and local communities. These recommendations will continue to be taken into account in ZELA's advocacy work beyond the project phase, to ensure that there is responsible and sustainable mining, in line with regional and international good practices.
